questions.prompt: If system A is in thermal equilibrium with system C, and system B is in thermal equilibrium with C, then A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other even if they never touch.
questions.explanation: This is the zeroth law. It is the reason a thermometer (system C) can stand in for direct contact between A and B.

questions.prompt: Convert 68°F to degrees Celsius. Give the answer in °C (exact whole number).
Which heat transfer mechanism is the only one that works through a vacuum?
choices: Radiation
Conduction
Natural convection
Forced convection
questions.explanation: Radiation uses electromagnetic waves and needs no medium; conduction needs contact and convection needs a moving fluid.

questions.prompt: How much heat is needed to raise 0.2 kg of water from 20°C to 60°C? Use c = 4186 J/(kg·K). Give the answer in joules.
Which of these are state quantities (they depend only on the system's current state, not on the path taken)?
choices: Internal energy U
Heat Q
Work W
Temperature T
questions.explanation: Heat and work are process quantities that depend on the path; internal energy and temperature describe the state itself.

questions.prompt: Match each process name to its defining condition.
questions.explanation: Each name labels the quantity that is held fixed (or, for adiabatic, the absence of heat flow).

questions.prompt: A gas expands at a constant pressure of 1.5×10⁵ Pa from 0.01 m³ to 0.03 m³. How much work does the gas do? Give the answer in joules.
questions.explanation: For an isobaric process W = PΔV = (1.5×10⁵)(0.02) = 3000 J.

questions.prompt: Compared with an isothermal curve through the same starting point on a PV diagram, an adiabatic curve for an ideal gas is:
choices: Steeper, because PVᵞ = constant with γ > 1
Less steep, because no heat flows
Identical, since both involve an ideal gas
A vertical line
questions.answer: Steeper, because PVᵞ = constant with γ > 1
questions.explanation: Since γ > 1, pressure changes faster along PVᵞ = const than along PV = const.

questions.prompt: Explain why the net work done by a gas over one complete cycle equals the area enclosed by the loop on a PV diagram, and what the direction of travel (clockwise or counterclockwise) tells you.
rubric: Says legs with increasing volume add positive work and legs with decreasing volume subtract work
Says what remains is the enclosed area
Says clockwise gives positive net work done by the gas
Says counterclockwise gives negative net work (work done on the gas)
questions.model: Each leg contributes W = ∫P dV, the area under its path. Expanding legs add area and compressing legs subtract it, so around a closed loop what is left is the enclosed area. A clockwise loop gives positive net work done by the gas (a heat engine); a counterclockwise loop gives negative net work, meaning work is done on the gas (a refrigerator or heat pump).
questions.explanation: Net work is the area between the expansion and compression paths, with its sign set by the direction of travel.

questions.prompt: A gas absorbs 900 J of heat during a reversible isothermal process at 300 K. What is its entropy change in J/K?
questions.explanation: For an isothermal reversible process ΔS = Q/T = 900/300 = 3 J/K.

questions.prompt: Entropy tends to increase because higher-multiplicity macrostates are overwhelmingly more probable, not because the microscopic laws prefer a direction in time.
questions.explanation: The arrow of time is statistical: there are far more microstates for the disordered macrostate, so it is overwhelmingly likely.

questions.prompt: What one-word term describes an idealized process that is infinitely slow and dissipation-free, so it can be run exactly backward leaving no trace?
questions.explanation: A reversible process is a quasi-static, frictionless limit that real processes can only approach.

questions.prompt: A Carnot engine runs between a hot reservoir at 500 K and a cold reservoir at 300 K. What is its maximum efficiency, as a decimal (for example 0.25)?
Why can the coefficient of performance (COP) of a heat pump exceed 1 without violating any law?
choices: COP measures heat moved per unit of work, not work out per heat in
COP is measured in Kelvin, so it can be large
A heat pump creates extra energy from the environment
The second law does not apply to heat pumps
questions.answer: COP measures heat moved per unit of work, not work out per heat in
questions.explanation: A heat pump moves existing heat rather than converting energy, so Q/W is not capped at 1 like engine efficiency.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity to its formula.
questions.explanation: Efficiency is work out per heat in; refrigerator COP counts heat removed from the cold side; heat pump COP counts heat delivered to the hot side.

questions.prompt: Put the segments of a heating curve for ice at constant pressure in order, starting from solid ice below 0°C.
questions.explanation: Temperature climbs within each phase and stays flat during each phase change while latent heat is absorbed.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the van der Waals equation (P + an²/V²)(V − nb) = nRT are correct?
choices: b accounts for the volume the molecules themselves occupy
The an²/V² term corrects for attractive forces between molecules
Setting a = 0 and b = 0 recovers PV = nRT
It predicts that the ideal gas law becomes more accurate at high pressure and low temperature
answers: b accounts for the volume the molecules themselves occupy
The an²/V² term corrects for attractive forces between molecules
Setting a = 0 and b = 0 recovers PV = nRT
questions.explanation: The ideal gas law breaks down at high pressure and low temperature, which is exactly where the corrections matter.

questions.prompt: Name the three independent layers that stop any real engine from reaching 100% efficiency.
rubric: Kelvin statement forbids Q_c = 0, so e < 1
Carnot ceiling e = 1 − Tc/Th caps even the ideal case
Real processes are irreversible and generate entropy, so actual efficiency falls below the Carnot limit
questions.model: First, the Kelvin statement forbids an engine with Q_c = 0, so efficiency is always below 1. Second, the Carnot ceiling 1 − Tc/Th limits even a perfect reversible engine to less than 1. Third, real engines are irreversible and generate entropy, so they fall short of even the Carnot limit.
questions.explanation: Each layer is a consequence of the second law, so none can be removed by better engineering.
